title: The Old Stone Bridge
summary: A crumbling single-span bridge over a narrow river gorge. Locals swear they hear footsteps crossing at night, but the bridge is always empty when they look.
body: A crumbling single-span bridge arches over a narrow river gorge. The stone is slick with moss and the parapet is chipped where carts have scraped it for generations.

After sundown, locals claim they hear footsteps and the creak of unseen weight crossing from bank to bank. Lantern light shows nothing, and any attempt to wait on the bridge feels like being watched from below.
Use this as a travel encounter that can turn into combat, negotiation, or a social mystery depending on what is haunting the bridge.
hooks: Travelers vanish when crossing after sundown.
A rival party swears they were pushed by an invisible hand mid-crossing.
A local begs the party to retrieve a charm tossed into the river years ago.
complications: The bridge shudders and cracks if angered or disrespected.
The river below carries bones and broken gear from past incidents.
The haunting is a misdirect for something living under the water.
rewards: A hidden cache wedged under a loose stone.
A blessing for safe crossing in this region.
A clue pointing to a larger threat upstream.

title: Mistwatch Tower
special_element: When the sun breaks through, the tower goes, and it takes whatever is inside with it. Its residents and anyone still within its walls are not killed. They are taken, and they don't reappear anywhere on the ridge. They are gone as completely as the stone, until someone comes up on another foggy morning to fetch them.
summary: Category: Location · Region: state2 · Difficulty: medium · Mood: mysterious
body: Category: Location · Region: state2 · Difficulty: medium · Mood: mysterious

On clear days the ridge is bare. But come a grey, wet dawn and the Mistwatch Tower is simply *there*: black stone streaked with damp, its door hanging open, and a smell of cold ash drifting down the slope as though someone left a fire an hour ago. Somewhere above, a bell no one has rung creaks once on its chain.

The tower exists only while the fog holds. In full sun the ridge is heather and a few flattened stones. There is no foundation, no rubble, nothing to dig for. At dawn, in fog thick enough to blind a hawk, the tower stands exactly where it always stands, with its door open and the hearth still grey with ash.

Locals do their ridge business on clear mornings only. The few who have gone up in fog say the watch-room is ordinary: a table, sleeping pallets, a cold hearth. But everything looks as if someone stepped out a moment ago. A cup sits half full, and the surface of the water is still rippling. The stair is another matter. It climbs higher than the tower is tall, and people who go up there don't stay past the first turn. The tower isn't an abandoned post. Nobody walked out of it. The building and everyone in it were taken together, and the weather decides when it happens next.
Nobody knows when the fog will burn off. It can hold for an hour, or it can lift in the time it takes to climb the stair.

Decide before play how much warning the party gets before the fog lifts: the birdsong going quiet, the grey paling to white, or nothing at all. That choice is where the tension of this location comes from. The truth behind the vanishing is simple. The taken are not dead. They stand unaged on the stair, and none of them can find the way down alone. Anyone who climbs up on a foggy morning and leads them down by the hand can bring them out, but only one or two at a time, and slowly. Every trip back up is another chance for the sun to break through and take the rescuer as well.

Special element: When the sun breaks through, the tower goes, and it takes whatever is inside with it. Its residents and anyone still within its walls are not killed. They are taken, and they don't reappear anywhere on the ridge. They are gone as completely as the stone, until someone comes up on another foggy morning to fetch them.
complications: Hooks: a shepherd went up in fog after a dog lost three winters ago and came back down with it, not a day older. He swears there were people standing on the stair above it, and one of them asked him the date. A mother pays well for anyone willing to search the tower at dawn for her son, who went up years ago and never came down.

Complications: from inside, nobody can tell when the fog will lift. Only someone outside can judge it, and shouts from outside don't carry through the tower's walls. The party will need a signal they have agreed in advance: a lantern in a window, or a rope tied to the door-ring.

Rewards: decades of untouched supplies fill the watch-room. There is also a logbook of travellers who sheltered here, and each name ends mid-entry on a foggy date. One of the names belongs to the mother's son, and his last line says he was going up the stair.

title: Skull Marsh Causeway
special_element: The skulls are a compass that has always been honest, and someone has begun quietly turning them. No fog, no ambush, nothing in the water — just a few inches of rotation on a dead man's head, done overnight, and the safest road on the crossing becomes the fastest way to drown.
summary: Category: Location · Region: state2 · Biome: marsh · Difficulty: medium · Mood: grim
body: Category: Location · Region: state2 · Biome: marsh · Difficulty: medium · Mood: grim

A causeway of fitted grey stone runs dead straight through the marsh, sunk to the ankle in black water on either side. Every twenty paces a post rises from the muck, topped with a skull — real bone, weathered to the colour of driftwood. The air tastes of standing water and rot. Every skull you pass is facing the causeway. Not the marsh. The road.

The causeway is the only dry crossing through six miles of drowned marsh, laid down by marsh-folk generations back over ground too soft to trust. The skulls are their own drowned dead, set to face the firm footing so the departed could go on showing the living the way home.

Keep to the line the skulls face and the far side comes up dry-booted in under an hour. Step off it and the road stops being a road: the stone shelves crumble underfoot, and the marsh takes a boot, then a leg, before it lets go.
In the northern third, a handful of skulls have been turned — some a few degrees, one nearly backward — so the line they mark now runs off the stone and straight into the mire.

Decide before play who is turning the skulls and how much surfaces here. The causeway stands alone as a hazard the party beats by careful observation, or it opens straight into a pursuit as the first scene of a longer investigation. If your table has already made the crossing at Greymarch, keep the two distinct: that causeway is a road that must be read, this one is a road that has been edited, and the danger is entirely in the hand that moved the bone. *Variant:* if you want the marsh itself culpable, let the turned skulls face the deepest water and leave no footprints — but pick one and commit; a vandal and a haunting at once dulls both. Either way, name no culprit in read-aloud text. Let them walk the line and notice the wrongness themselves.

Special element: The skulls are a compass that has always been honest, and someone has begun quietly turning them. No fog, no ambush, nothing in the water — just a few inches of rotation on a dead man's head, done overnight, and the safest road on the crossing becomes the fastest way to drown.
complications: Hooks: a courier is three days overdue on a one-day route; a marsh-folk elder asks outsiders to walk the line and report which skulls have moved; a merchant offers coin to anyone who'll "fix" the markers, no questions asked.
Complications: night or fog, when a turned skull is near-impossible to catch by eye; the causeway's warden insists nothing is wrong and turns evasive when pressed.
Rewards: safe passage and the marsh-folk's goodwill for resetting the markers; a name, a footprint, or a dropped tool at the base of a turned post — a thread toward whoever is turning them.

title: Emberglass Cavern
special_element: **The cavern runs hotter with depth, and the heat is stored, not made.** No fire burns down there, no mineral vein explains it. The glass holds warmth the way a hearth does after the flame has gone out — and the deeper you go, the older and stronger that borrowed warmth gets. Whatever banked it did so a very long time ago, and it has not cooled.
summary: Category: Location · Tier: 2 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: cavern · Mood: wondrous
body: Category: Location · Tier: 2 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: cavern · Mood: wondrous

The tunnel narrows, then opens into a cave built of black glass. Every wall is soot-dark crystal, faceted like a thousand mirrors turned away from the light, and the air is warm — not damp cave-warm, but *hearth*-warm, the way a room feels after the fire's been going all afternoon. Torchlight comes back off the facets gold instead of white.
Walk deeper and the warmth climbs. A cave should get colder the further you go from the sky. This one doesn't.

Emberglass Cavern is a vein of glassy black stone that formed, by all evidence, around something that burned for a very long time. Prospectors who mapped the outer chambers found the crystal cool to the touch at the mouth and close to skin-scalding two hundred feet in — a gradient that runs backwards from every cave anyone has surveyed.

The glass fractures into curved, obsidian-sharp shards. Miners working the outer seams describe a low, resiny warmth coming off a freshly-broken face, like standing too close to banked coals. Nobody has mapped the deep chambers and come back with a full account of what is down there.

Decide before play what banked the heat at the bottom of the gradient — a dormant elemental, a buried forge from an age nobody remembers, or nothing at all, just glass that remembers fire the way old wood remembers the axe. None of it needs revealing on this visit. The gradient is the hook; the answer is the second visit.

Push the heat as a real cost past two hundred feet: exhaustion, water skins gone hot and foul, glass too hot to grip bare-handed. Rule the deep chambers as difficult terrain for anyone in metal armour. This is a hard site because the environment is the antagonist — there is no monster waiting in the dark unless you put one there.

Special element: **The cavern runs hotter with depth, and the heat is stored, not made.** No fire burns down there, no mineral vein explains it. The glass holds warmth the way a hearth does after the flame has gone out — and the deeper you go, the older and stronger that borrowed warmth gets. Whatever banked it did so a very long time ago, and it has not cooled.
complications: Hooks: a mining concern wants a survey team to find how deep the warm seam runs; a scholar insists the reversed gradient breaks a law of nature and wants first-hand notes; the prospector who went furthest in came back and will not say what the heat sounded like.
Complications: shards fracture underfoot and open thin cuts that cauterise as they open; the thickened air slows any spell needing a clear breath; torches sweat and gutter near the hottest walls.
Rewards: raw emberglass sells well to jewellers and alchemists for its colour; a fist-sized shard cut from the deep chambers stays warm in the hand for days.

title: Market of Quiet Coins
special_element: Price here is set by the secret a buyer is carrying, not by their coin. A vendor can tell by looking whether you hold something worth knowing, and the price drops the nearer you come to saying it aloud. Pay in coin alone and everything costs full, or more. Let something slip — even sideways, even by accident — and the vendor's ledger has already written it down before you finish the sentence.
summary: Category: Location · Region: state5 · Difficulty: medium · Mood: mysterious
body: Category: Location · Region: state5 · Difficulty: medium · Mood: mysterious

The Market of Quiet Coins opens after dark, in a square that carries no name on any daylight map. The stalls light one at a time, each under a single low lantern, and the air runs hot oil, then brine, then — underneath both — ink. Nobody calls out their wares. The vendors wait for you to come to them, and they are already turning toward you before you move.

By day the square is nothing: cracked flagstones, a dry fountain, three shuttered fronts. After dusk the merchants do not arrive so much as become present, laying out dried fish and good rope and plain daggers beside a bottled storm and a key that opens locks it has never touched.

Buyers drift between the stalls without speaking. The silence is the market's working condition, not its atmosphere — haggling here is not done with words, and a vendor who hears too much talk simply folds the cloth over their goods.
Ask the price of anything and the vendor names a number, holds your face a beat too long, and quietly names a smaller one.

Decide before play what the market is fishing for — a named NPC's whereabouts, a player character's hidden guilt, one piece of world-shaking lore — and give one vendor that exact target. Play the silence straight: no vendor explains the rule, no vendor asks a question, and none of them ever say the word "secret." The players should work it out from the second discount.

This page is the market as a place to *buy* — the pressure is on what the party is willing to say out loud; run **The Night Market Heist** instead when they mean to take something off the stalls rather than pay for it. *Variant: if you want the market hostile rather than eerie, let a vendor read a secret off a character who never speaks at all — purchase by proximity.*

Special element: Price here is set by the secret a buyer is carrying, not by their coin. A vendor can tell by looking whether you hold something worth knowing, and the price drops the nearer you come to saying it aloud. Pay in coin alone and everything costs full, or more. Let something slip — even sideways, even by accident — and the vendor's ledger has already written it down before you finish the sentence.
complications: Hooks: a party member's belonging is laid out for sale here four days before it is stolen; a vendor offers a discount steep enough to be an accusation, because they have named the exact secret they want.
Complications: a sold secret belongs to the stall, and the stall sells it on to whoever comes next; the market is gone at first light, and so is any bargain left half-struck.
Rewards: goods that exist nowhere else; information bought the same way it was sold — one secret out for one secret in.

title: Tideworn Chapel
special_element: The chapel rebuilds its interior — altar, icon, offerings, and the blank face of the statue — to answer whatever the person walking through the door most needs, and it has never once guessed wrong. Nobody has worked out how it knows.
summary: Category: Location · Tier: 1 · Biome: coast · Difficulty: easy · Mood: wondrous
body: Category: Location · Tier: 1 · Biome: coast · Difficulty: easy · Mood: wondrous

A small stone chapel sits above the tideline, its driftwood pews bleached grey, salt crusting every sill. Inside, you can hear the sea — a slow wash and pull, in and out — though the water is fifty feet below and the door has been shut all winter. The air smells of wax and brine. Over the altar stands a carved figure whose face was never finished: smooth stone where the features should be.
Fishing families up and down the coast use the chapel, and none of them agree on which god it belongs to. Ask three worshippers and you get three answers, each delivered with total confidence.
They are not lying. No one enters the chapel the same way twice. Between visits the building keeps its walls, its pews, and the sound of the sea — everything else moves.

A sailor finds carved fish heaped for a sea-mother. A widow finds a shrine hung with mourning cloth cut for her exact loss. A child looking for courage finds a painted knight above the altar. No one has ever caught it changing. The door opens and it is already different.
The chapel is not the Red Stag Trail. The Trail moves you toward the thing you want and charges you for the walk; the chapel gives nothing, takes nothing, and only says the thing out loud.

Decide before play what the chapel shows each visiting character, and why — it must reflect something true about them, not a random image. The chapel grants insight, never mechanical benefit; resist turning it into a vending machine for buffs and answers. The pressure here is social, not tactical: the cost of entering is that your party sees what you needed. Variant: if you want the place hungrier, let the statue's face finish itself a little more with every visitor it reads correctly.

Special element: The chapel rebuilds its interior — altar, icon, offerings, and the blank face of the statue — to answer whatever the person walking through the door most needs, and it has never once guessed wrong. Nobody has worked out how it knows.
complications: Hooks: a grieving villager insists the party visit "their" chapel and see what it shows them; a scholar pays good coin to anyone who can catch the interior changing.
Complications: two characters enter together and each sees a different room; argue about it in front of the statue and the doors seal until the arguing stops.

Rewards: the room a character walks into names a truth they had never said aloud — and it names it in front of whoever came in with them. The party leaves knowing something about each other they were not told: a rumour, a place, or a piece of a companion's past.

title: Red Stag Trail
special_element: The trail leads each walker, separately, toward the thing they most want — and it splits the party without any of them noticing. Five people set off shoulder to shoulder, certain they never lost sight of each other, and arrive at five different places hours apart. Only afterward, comparing the walk, does anyone realise they were never on the same path at all.
summary: Category: Location · Tier: 2 · Biome: forest · Difficulty: medium · Mood: mysterious
body: Category: Location · Tier: 2 · Biome: forest · Difficulty: medium · Mood: mysterious

The trail is barely a trail — a deer-track of packed leaf-mould, silent underfoot, smelling of wet bark and something sweeter beneath it, like fruit left too long in the sun. Sunlight comes down in coin-sized patches. And somewhere behind you, without anyone ever deciding to stop talking, your companions have gone quiet.

The Red Stag Trail runs through a stretch of ancient forest that no two maps agree on. Locals know not to walk it alone, and know better than to walk it in a hurry. It is not lost — it simply does not go where you think it goes.

Travellers describe walking single file for an afternoon and arriving somewhere none of them meant to. A hunter chasing a stag comes out at the edge of a lake he swears was never in this wood. A merchant taking a shortcut to market steps out an hour later at his own front door.
Nothing on the trail attacks. Whatever tends it wants people walking, not running.

Decide before play what each PC's "want" resolves to — keep it small and personal (a person, a place, an answer), not campaign-ending. Use the split to peel one PC away for a private scene, or to quietly reunite the party if their wants align. Never announce the split; let the players find it when someone says "wait — when did we get here?" Variant: run the trail as a single shared path that leads only to the party's loudest want, if you'd rather not break the group up.

Special element: The trail leads each walker, separately, toward the thing they most want — and it splits the party without any of them noticing. Five people set off shoulder to shoulder, certain they never lost sight of each other, and arrive at five different places hours apart. Only afterward, comparing the walk, does anyone realise they were never on the same path at all.
complications: Hooks: a search party insists their missing hunter "just walked into the trees and never came out the other side"; a merchant caravan hires an escort through the wood and doesn't know to warn anyone.
Complications: a PC's own want pulls them off course mid-scene, with no moment where the group actually separated; whatever the party is chasing may have left the same way.
Rewards: a walker who reaches what they wanted sometimes finds it waiting, faintly changed — a lost person, a lost coin, a lost certainty — and the wood asks nothing for it. Yet.

title: Library of Salt
special_element: Every shape in the salt drifts was once a person who read too long. The library preserves its readers the way it preserves its pages — slowly, from the fingertips inward — and every hour spent absorbed in a text is an hour spent becoming one more curve in the floor. There is no ritual and no curse to break. It is simply patient, and it is still hungry.
summary: Category: Location · Tier: 3 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: ruins · Mood: melancholy
body: Category: Location · Tier: 3 · Difficulty: hard · Biome: ruins · Mood: melancholy

Salt has swallowed the Library of Salt. The shelves are sagging white ridges now, crusted thick as bone, sloping down into drifts that reach the knee. The air tastes of brine before it tastes of anything else — dry, mineral, catching at the back of the throat with every breath. The drifts underfoot do not shift like sand. They hold their shape: a curve here like a bent shoulder, a hollow there like a cupped hand, pressed into the salt and never disturbed. No wind moves through the broken roof, and yet, somewhere below the floor, the salt sighs.

Before the collapse this was a great reading hall — vaulted stone, shelving from floor to ceiling, a place scholars travelled seasons to reach. What toppled it wasn't fire or war. The salt came from within, seeping up through the floor stones over decades: first a fine crust on the lowest shelves, then drifts that buried whole aisles. Most of the books are gone, dissolved or entombed. What's left are salt-white pages, brittle as old bone, scattered loose across the ridgelines.

The hall is treacherous. Ceiling sections groan and shed dust at a raised voice, and a drift-bank can slump and swallow a careless step. Torch flame leans and gutters in the salt-damp air for no reason the DM needs to explain.

Anyone who stays and reads — really reads, page after page, hour after hour — starts to notice their own knuckles drying, their voice roughening like a throat full of dust. The library does not want visitors. It wants readers who don't leave.

Decide before play how long a character can read before the salt starts taking them — a clean, visible countdown (one mark per hour of in-fiction reading) works better than a hidden save. Let the players watch a companion's hand pale and stiffen well before it matters mechanically; the horror is in seeing it happen, not in the moment it's confirmed. This is the site the *Salt That Was Words* and the *Salt-Sheet Riddle* were dug out of, not a retelling of either: the lore is where the salt came from, the riddle is one page read closely, and this place is what the reading costs by the hour. Run it cold — neither is required at the table.

Special element: Every shape in the salt drifts was once a person who read too long. The library preserves its readers the way it preserves its pages — slowly, from the fingertips inward — and every hour spent absorbed in a text is an hour spent becoming one more curve in the floor. There is no ritual and no curse to break. It is simply patient, and it is still hungry.
complications: Hooks: a scholar's family hires the party to retrieve someone who went in three weeks ago and never came out · a fragment of salt-page turns up in a market stall, still faintly legible.
Complications: a character becomes absorbed in a text and loses track of time — track it openly, in hours, not narrative beats · the ceiling sheds a section if anyone shouts or fights inside.

Rewards: intact salt-pages hold genuinely lost knowledge, worth real coin to the right buyer · one drift, excavated carefully, yields a reader's untouched satchel — their tools, their notes, their name.

title: Hollow Ward Post
special_element: Travellers who spend the night hear the bell ring once before dawn: a single clear toll from above the empty lintel. The warning is always true. Whatever danger the road holds that day — a predator on the trail, a washed-out ford, a patrol with wrong intentions — the bell rings first. Nobody who passes through asks about it twice.
summary: Category: Location · Region: state1 · Difficulty: easy · Mood: unsettling
body: Category: Location · Region: state1 · Difficulty: easy · Mood: unsettling

A squat stone post where the frontier road narrows — walls the colour of old ash, a rusted iron bracket above the lintel where a bell once hung. Inside, woodsmoke and sage still hang in the air, and the kettle on its hook holds water warm to the touch. The hearth holds only cold grey ash. There is no other door.

The waypost was built to log traveller traffic on the frontier road, and it did, for a generation. The Frontier Watch was disbanded — nobody out here agrees on exactly when — and the post was quietly abandoned. Travellers still use it as a shelter, and whatever they find inside, they leave as they found it. Out here that habit has a name: *the customs of the road.*
A duty ledger hangs on a peg by the door. The last signed entry is dated three weeks ago, and the page is not quite full.
The iron bracket above the lintel held the alarm bell. It was taken down before the post closed — lost, repurposed, nobody agrees. The bracket has been empty for years.

Decide before play whether the bell rings that night. If it does, have something true waiting on the road — bad weather, a predator, an ambush. The bell is never a bluff: honour it every time, and the players learn to trust it. That trust is the hook.

The kettle and the bell are separate beats. Run *The Kettle's Still Warm* first if you want the post unsettling from the moment they arrive; let the bell come later, in the dark, after they have stopped wondering who made the fire.

Do not explain the bell unless the players pursue it hard. A partial answer — *"the old watch-captain who last rang it is buried on the ridge somewhere, they say"* — gives them something to hold without closing the question.

Special element: Travellers who spend the night hear the bell ring once before dawn: a single clear toll from above the empty lintel. The warning is always true. Whatever danger the road holds that day — a predator on the trail, a washed-out ford, a patrol with wrong intentions — the bell rings first. Nobody who passes through asks about it twice.
complications: **Hooks:** The ledger's last entry carries a name the party recognises. · The kettle is warm with no fire to explain it (→ *The Kettle's Still Warm*). · A bedroll on the bunk has been slept in since the last rain.

**Complications:** The bell rings mid-afternoon, not before dawn — something on the road ahead is not following the old rules. · A rider pulls in hard and fast, wanting walls between themselves and the road, not yet willing to say what is behind them.

**Rewards:** The ledger holds route notes going back years — terrain, flood dates, patrol schedules, warnings left by travellers who knew the road. · A sealed tin box under the bunk, addressed *DELIVER IF FOUND* to a name in a town two days east.

title: Black Lantern Bay
statblock:
AC 15 (natural armor) · HP 82 (11d10+22) · Speed 0 ft, swim 40 ft
STR 18  DEX 12  CON 14  INT 10  WIS 16  CHA 13
Skills: Perception +7, Stealth +5 (in water)
Key action: Anchoring Grasp — as a reaction, the Warden holds a Large or smaller vessel or creature in place; moving it at all that turn requires a Strength saving throw.
CR 5  (scale: easy = CR2, hard = CR7 — see Difficulty)
special_element: No ship in Black Lantern Bay is ever tied down, and no ship has ever drifted. A barrel dropped over the side rides off with the tide like anything else on ordinary water. A hull with its ropes coiled uselessly on deck stays exactly where it was set, through the same storms that have splintered piers up and down the coast. Something under the bay is holding the ships — deliberately, and gently. It wants them kept, not sunk. Which means every departure from this harbour is granted, and can be refused.
summary: Black Lantern Bay Category: Location · Region: state10 · Difficulty: hard · Mood: unsettling
body: Black Lantern Bay Category: Location · Region: state10 · Difficulty: hard · Mood: unsettling

The bay is quiet in a way harbours never are. Lanterns hang from the mooring posts and the bows of every ship, burning pale blue-white, and the air around them is colder than the air around them has any right to be. Frost feathers the mooring posts. It does not feather the ropes, because there are no ropes — every hull sits motionless at its berth, untied, unanchored, held still by nothing you can see.
Black Lantern Bay is the deepest natural harbour on this coast: sheltered water, easy soundings, room for forty hulls. It should be the busiest port for sixty miles. It is half-empty.

The lanterns are lit at dusk, and nobody has seen a hand do it. Touch one and the glass stings bare skin like packed snow, though the flame inside gutters and leans the way any ordinary fire does. Walk the pier from shore to end and the cold deepens with every plank, until the last twenty feet are winter regardless of the season.

Fish still school under the piers. Gulls still wheel and squabble over the shallows. Sailors who berth here speak of the place in short sentences and never sleep below deck two nights running — and they all know the harbourmaster's rule, which is that a ship leaves when the bay is finished with it and not before.

Decide before play what is anchoring the ships — a bound spirit, a pact the harbour town made generations ago and has forgotten the terms of, or something colder and less explicable. The answer never has to be spoken at the table. Play the bay as something making a decision about the party, and let them feel it decide whether they may leave.

If your table has met ships riding ropeless elsewhere on this coast, keep the distinction sharp: out there it is an incident and a mystery, here it is the standing condition of the harbour and the reason the berths are half-empty.
*Variant:* if you want the bay hostile rather than possessive, the presence is not keeping ships — it is collecting them, and the half-empty berths are the ones it has already finished with.

Special element: No ship in Black Lantern Bay is ever tied down, and no ship has ever drifted. A barrel dropped over the side rides off with the tide like anything else on ordinary water. A hull with its ropes coiled uselessly on deck stays exactly where it was set, through the same storms that have splintered piers up and down the coast. Something under the bay is holding the ships — deliberately, and gently. It wants them kept, not sunk. Which means every departure from this harbour is granted, and can be refused.
complications: Hooks: a captain pays well to learn why their ship will not leave its berth on their word alone; a body washes up in high summer with frost damage to the hands and face.

Complications: cutting a ship free by force draws the bay's attention — the cold deepens and the lanterns nearest that vessel gutter out, one by one, roughly one a minute. When the last of them dies the bay stops keeping that hull: it goes where the tide takes it, crew aboard or not, and it will never hold at this berth again. Anything thrown overboard after dark does not always sink.

Rewards: guaranteed harbour against any storm, for those the bay accepts — a hull it is holding cannot be driven aground, boarded off its moorings, or swept out; a salvager's fortune still in the holds of ships nobody has been brave enough to fully unload.

title: The Causeway at Greymarch
special_element: The ground hasn't forgotten it was a riverbed. Anything set down inside the old ford line — a dropped coin, an arrowhead, a boot heel pressed too long — sinks straight through the topsoil and is gone, swallowed the way a real current would take it, while the field above stays bone dry and the wheat never shows a mark. The Order isn't the haunting. The water is still there, underneath, exactly where it used to run.
summary: Category: Location · Region: state1 · Difficulty: easy · Mood: mysterious
body: Category: Location · Region: state1 · Difficulty: easy · Mood: mysterious

Wheat runs waist-high and gold to the horizon — except along one line, where it doesn't. There the stalks bend and part the way a current bends around a boot, though no water has run here in three hundred years. Stand at the field's edge at dusk and you'll hear boots strike stone. Then you'll see them: a dozen men in old plate, formed up in a rank with no living officer, guarding a crossing that isn't there.

Three centuries ago the Greymarch was a river, and this was its only ford. The Unfallen Order mustered here to hold the crossing against something the chronicles never name, and by every account they held it. The river silted out a generation later. Farmers ploughed the bed under.
What's left is ordinary wheat and an old rank of the Order, still turning out to guard a line of water that dried up before their own graves did.

The soldiers don't attack, don't speak first, and don't leave the exact width of the old ford — forty paces, no more. Approach from the field and they part like sentries used to a supply wagon. Try to cross that forty-pace strip on foot and they close it, polite and immovable, until you go around.

Decide before play whether this rank is the Unfallen Order still mustering, or a detachment left behind and forgotten by the Order proper — that changes whether word of trouble at the causeway ever reaches anyone who could answer it.
The buried river is mechanical, not dressing: treat the forty-pace strip as submerging terrain any time something is deliberately pushed into it, whatever the topsoil looks like.

If your table has already walked the Skull Marsh Causeway, name the difference out loud: there the water is visible and the road is sinking into it, and the danger is what you can see. Here the road is gone, the water is invisible, and the danger is ground that behaves like a current when nothing about it looks wet.

Special element: The ground hasn't forgotten it was a riverbed. Anything set down inside the old ford line — a dropped coin, an arrowhead, a boot heel pressed too long — sinks straight through the topsoil and is gone, swallowed the way a real current would take it, while the field above stays bone dry and the wheat never shows a mark. The Order isn't the haunting. The water is still there, underneath, exactly where it used to run.
complications: Hooks: A farmer's son waded into the wheat on a dare and hasn't come out; a merchant lost a strongbox "into the ground" at the ford line and wants it back.

Complications: Digging along the ford line collapses the soil into open, genuinely wet channel for a few minutes before it seals — anyone standing on the line when it opens goes under with the strongbox.
Rewards: Three centuries of lost goods sit in the buried channel — coin, a rusted standard of the Order, and, deeper down, a name-etched pauldron matching no soldier standing guard above.

title: Ashwell Chapel
special_element: The fifth mold is empty and uncast, and it is warm — blood-warm at rest, and hot enough to sting when the person it is waiting for comes within arm's reach of it. It is a plain offer, and the clerics will make it plainly: press a palm into the wax and let it take the cast. A fifth candle is lit that hour, and the Order holds vigil for you as it holds vigil for Aldous — die once, and the ground gives you back within a mile of wherever you fell. The price is the candle. It must burn, tended, for as long as you want the return. The Order tends it at no charge only while the Order trusts you. Let it gutter — by their choice or your enemies' — and the return is spent without ever being used.

The chapel of the Unfallen Order sits low against the frontier hedgerow, grey stone furred with lichen, its door never locked. Inside, the air smells of tallow and old rain. Four candle-stubs burn behind iron bars in a wall niche — flames that stand dead straight, though the door is open to the wind.

The Order keeps this chapel for one purpose: to hold vigil over a knight named Ser Aldous, who has died four times — each death entered in the parish ledger in a different hand — and each time risen from unmarked ground within a mile of the door.

Set into the east wall is an iron reliquary the size of a coffin. Inside sit four wax casts of a human hand, palm up, taken from Ser Aldous while the body was still cold. Each has a candle beside it. Behind them is a fifth mold. It has never been filled.
The four casts are Aldous's, and they are cold wax; his deaths are counted, kept, and paid for. The fifth mold is not his. It is waiting on a hand that has not died yet.

Clerics tend the four candles in rotation, day and night, and never leave one burning alone. They will tell you what a guttered candle costs, because it is the whole of their work: a cast whose candle goes out goes cold, that death stops counting, and the man loses a return.

Decide before play which PC the mold is warm for — pick the one with the most to lose, and let the warmth single them out in front of the table. The offer should be cheap to accept now and expensive to keep: a lit candle is a leash as much as a life. Name the cleric who would tend it; the Order withdrawing that service, or an enemy learning where the candle burns, is a consequence you can spend later. If nobody accepts, nothing is wasted — the mold keeps warming, and the party leaves carrying a standing offer rather than a locked box.

Special element: The fifth mold is empty and uncast, and it is warm — blood-warm at rest, and hot enough to sting when the person it is waiting for comes within arm's reach of it. A fifth candle is lit that hour, and the Order holds vigil for you as it holds vigil for Aldous — die once, and the ground gives you back within a mile of wherever you fell. The price is the candle. It must burn, tended, for as long as you want the return. The Order tends it at no charge only while the Order trusts you. Let it gutter — by their choice or your enemies' — and the return is spent without ever being used.
complications: Hooks: the party is hired to keep the vigil for one night; a cleric goes missing and the rotation breaks, so a cast is cooling and must be re-lit before dawn or Aldous loses a return; a stranger asks to be left alone with the reliquary and is found later with wax under their fingernails.

Complications: a candle gutters while the party is present and the clerics ask one of them to fill the fifth mold to keep the vigil unbroken; the mold scalds exactly one PC and stays cool for the others, in front of witnesses who now know it; Ser Aldous rides in himself and asks who has been handling his reliquary.

Rewards: a cast in the fifth mold — one death undone, so long as the candle burns; the Order's trust and safe harbour on the frontier; a copied page from the parish ledger; a spare wax hand-cast as a keepsake, still faintly warm days later.

title: Callow's Ford
special_element: The ruin still keeps its schedule. Every dusk Callow's Ford runs its last evening again, from the first lamp to the hour the fire started. When the lamps light, the town stands again: doors, stairs and the bell tower whole, just for the evening. At midnight the bell stops ringing three notes and starts ringing the alarm. That is when the evening ends. Anyone still inside a lit building at the alarm wakes at the next dusk, lying in the ash where that building stood, with a full day gone and the smell of smoke in their hair. Most ghosts repeat a moment. Callow's Ford keeps a timetable, and the party can be late for it.

Ash-grey foundations line the ford road: stone footings and black stubs of timber, none of it higher than your knee. The air still smells of char, fifty years after a fire should have taken the smell with it. Downstream a red-painted waterwheel turns slowly and creaks over a streambed that has been dry for a generation. Halfway down the ruined street one building stands whole, with its roof on and a lamp burning gold in the front window.

Callow's Ford was a garrison town at the river crossing until the fire took it. Foundations, a well and the stone stub of a bell tower are all that's left. People in the nearest village won't cross the ford after dark. They won't say why, only that "the Ford keeps its own hours."

The bell tower still has its bell. It rings three clean notes on the hour. The rope rotted through long ago, and no one has climbed to the platform in living memory. The waterwheel turns in time with the bell and drives nothing.

The one whole building is an inn. Its lamp is always lit and its door is never locked. Anyone who steps inside finds a fire in the grate, supper on the table, and a woman who calls them by a name that isn't theirs.

Before play, decide one thing: when the party tells her the truth, does the Widow go out with the lamps, or is she left standing in the ash, alive and fifty years late? Either works; the choice sets the tone. Don't explain the mechanism. Let the players hear the bell before they see the lamp, and let the lamp be what makes them go and look. Count the bells out loud once the lamps are lit.

Special element: The ruin still keeps its schedule. Every dusk Callow's Ford runs its last evening again, from the first lamp to the hour the fire started. When the lamps light, the town stands again: doors, stairs and the bell tower whole, just for the evening. At midnight the bell stops ringing three notes and starts ringing the alarm. That is when the evening ends. Anyone still inside a lit building at the alarm wakes at the next dusk, lying in the ash where that building stood, with a full day gone and the smell of smoke in their hair. Most ghosts repeat a moment. Callow's Ford keeps a timetable, and the party can be late for it.
complications: Hooks: a letter reaches someone in the party, ink still wet and dated the evening before the fire, written by the keeper of the Callow's Ford inn and asking for them by a name that isn't theirs. Rumour says the garrison payroll, missing since the fire, is still in the strongroom under the bell tower.

Complications: by day the strongroom is buried under fallen stone. It can only be reached after dusk, through the tower door the evening puts back, and the clock is running from the moment the lamps light. The Widow Sarn, the woman in the inn, believes it is still the evening before the fire. She holds the strongroom key for the garrison, and she will only hand it to the person she thinks the party member is.

Rewards: the garrison's last payroll lies untouched in the strongroom. There are two ways to get the key, and each costs something. Answer to the wrong name and she gives the key gladly, but she sets that PC a place at supper and holds them to it, which makes leaving before the alarm a matter of social skill or plain rudeness. Tell her what year it is and she believes it by the third bell. She gives the key freely, and when the party leaves, the lamps go out behind them and never light again: no second visit, no second try at the strongroom.
